Who

Retail girl
turned
brand girl

I came up through retail and never got far from the customer. I started on the floor of a boutique in Charleston — styling people, keeping the displays honest, shooting the content that got them through the door.

Then five years at a digital agency, auditing hundreds of brands and identifying where they were leaving growth on the table. I learned how to quickly understand a business, find the friction, and turn what I saw into a strategy people could actually get behind.

Now I'm brand-side. At Remu Apparel, a DTC menswear label, I own social, email, and ecommerce end to end — I concept it, shoot it, write it, build it, ship it. I'm relocating to New York City and looking for a team where I can bring that mix of customer instinct, marketing strategy, and hands-on execution to brands I believe in — whether that's fashion, beauty, CPG, or a boutique agency working across luxury and lifestyle clients.

Sézane — creator brief

Concept work · on spec

An unsolicited partnership brief for Sézane's U.S. influence team: a La Rentrée campaign concept, the mood, three shortlisted East Coast creators with the casting logic behind each, a four-step gifting rollout, and the talking points for outreach. The creator profiles are illustrative — the point was to show how I'd source and how I'd think.

Concept brand · self-initiated

Ají is the Ecuadorian hot sauce that sits on every table, and casero means homemade. I built the brand around it end to end as a concept — name, positioning, identity, label, and packaging, down to the line that carries the whole thing: born in Ecuador, made for everywhere. Nobody hired me to make this. I wanted to find out whether I could take a CPG brand from a blank page all the way to a shelf myself.

Three Altitudes

The Pintor, the Fogata, the Tambo

Ecuador is narrow enough to drive across in a day, and tall enough that you'll change clothes three times doing it.

That's not a metaphor. You leave Quito in the morning in one jacket, you're in a different one by the time the valley opens up, and if you keep going up you'll want heavy wool. Three of the pieces in this drop come from those three places.

2,850 m

Quito

The Pintor, in blue

pintor — painter

Quito sits at 2,850 meters, which means the sun is fierce by ten and gone by six, and the temperature does whatever it likes in between. You need one jacket you can leave on.

Named after a painter's coat — deep pockets, cut close, and built for getting things done. It's the one I reach for on a normal day.

See the Pintor →

$215 · M, L, XL

3,000 m

Machachi Valley

The Fogata, in olive

fogata — bonfire

An hour south the valley opens and the volcanoes line up on both sides. The moment the sun clears the ridge, the temperature drops — you feel it in about a minute — but nobody goes inside. Someone gets a fire going instead.

I made this for that hour. It's a mid layer, cut with room to go over a shirt.

See the Fogata →

$235 · L, XL, XXL

3,500 m

The páramo

The Tambo, in bordeaux

tambo — a wayside inn on the Inca roads

A tambo was a rest house. The Inca built them along their roads about a day's walk apart — somewhere to eat and sleep before moving on. Those roads crossed the páramo, the high grassland above the treeline where it's cold all year and the wind doesn't let up.

The tambo jacket is as reliable as its namesake, made from handspun wool.
